name: Thermal Processing vs. Washing for Cyclospora Produce Safety
anchorClaim: Thermal processing of fresh agricultural produce (encompassing all varieties of fruits and vegetables), specifically achieving a sustained internal temperature of at least 158°F (70°C) for a minimum of 2 minutes, achieves a >99.9% (3-log) inactivation of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts, whereas applying the maximum standard commercial and consumer washing protocols fails to achieve even a 99% (2-log) reduction on those same items.
plainQuestion: Heating produce to a safe cooking temperature kills Cyclospora, a parasite that causes serious diarrheal illness, better than washing does.
confidenceSummary: Grade D reflects a limited evidence base with only 9 direct tests and a near-even split between supporting and contradicting findings. The narrow majority is not enough to resolve the question.

guide.whatScienceSays: DATOM looked at 9 studies that directly tested this claim. Of those, 5 (56%) support the idea that heating produce to a safe cooking temperature kills Cyclospora better than washing does; 4 (44%) point the other way. So the clear findings are split nearly down the middle, which is what the "Contested" verdict below means. The Grade D beside it matters just as much: this is a limited evidence base with only 9 direct tests, so the question remains open. Many more studies touched on the topic without testing this exact claim; they appear further down, tagged by what they looked at.
guide.howConfident:
The 56% support share suggests a slight lean toward the claim, but 9 studies is a small pool and 4 contradicting findings is enough to create real uncertainty. A contested verdict reflects this near-even split rather than treating a bare majority as decisive.

The Grade D signals that the evidence base is limited in size. With only 9 direct tests and nearly half pointing against the claim, we cannot treat this as a settled question. The gap between a slim numerical majority and the contested grade reflects the fact that scientific confidence requires more than a coin-flip margin.
decisionSupport: Five studies found that heating produce to safe cooking temperatures kills Cyclospora more effectively than washing alone.
Four studies found that washing performs as well as or better than heating for eliminating Cyclospora from produce.
The 56% support rate represents a narrow majority, with nearly half of direct tests contradicting the claim.
Only 9 studies directly tested the comparative effectiveness of heating versus washing against Cyclospora.
The limited number of direct tests and the near-even split prevent a clear determination of which method is superior.
guide.faultLines:
Method comparison design: Some studies tested heating and washing as standalone interventions while others examined them in combination or sequence, making direct comparisons difficult. Studies that tested washing followed by heating may show different results than those testing each method alone.

Temperature and duration variation: Safe cooking temperature can mean different things across studies, from brief surface heating to thorough cooking at sustained high temperatures. Washing protocols also vary widely, from quick rinses to extended scrubbing with different water temperatures and pressures.

Produce type differences: Cyclospora may respond differently to heating and washing depending on the produce surface. Smooth-skinned vegetables like tomatoes may release parasites more easily during washing than leafy greens with complex surfaces, while heating effectiveness may depend on produce thickness and water content.

datoms.claim: Microwave heating inactivates Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts with measurable reduction in sporulation and viability.
datoms.source: Ynés R. Ortega, Jye‐Yin Liao "Microwave Inactivation of Cyclospora cayetanensis Sporulation and Viability of Cryptosporidium parvum Oocysts" (2006). doi:10.4315/0362-028x-69.8.1957

datoms.claim: High hydrostatic pressure treatment of produce contaminated with Eimeria acervulina (a Cyclospora cayetanensis surrogate) achieves measurable inactivation of oocysts.
datoms.source: Kalmia E. Kniel, Adrienne E.H. Shearer, Jennifer L. Cascarino, G. C. Wilkins, Mark C. Jenkins "High Hydrostatic Pressure and UV Light Treatment of Produce Contaminated with Eimeria acervulina as a Cyclospora cayetanensis Surrogate" (2007). doi:10.4315/0362-028x-70.12.2837

datoms.claim: Thermal processing at 70°C for 2 minutes does not achieve >99.9% (3-log) inactivation of Clostridioides difficile spores in milk.
datoms.source: Gizem Taylan Yalçın, Melike Nur Tosun Demir, Nükhet Nilüfer Demirel Zorba "High thermal resistance and inactivation behaviour of Clostridioides difficile spores in milk." (2026). doi:10.1007/s42770-026-01975-z

datoms.claim: Thermal processing at 70°C for 2 minutes achieves >99.9% (3-log) inactivation of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts in fresh produce.
datoms.source: Ynés R. Ortega, Lucy J. Robertson "Assessing and Controlling the Risk of Cyclospora cayetanensis in the Food-Chain" (2017). doi:10.1007/978-3-319-53587-6_7

datoms.claim: Heating Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts to 70°C prevents sporulation (an indicator of viability) in basil and water substrates.
datoms.source: Lakshmi Sathyanarayanan, Ynés R. Ortega "EFFECTS OF TEMPERATURE AND DIFFERENT FOOD MATRICES ON CYCLOSPORA CAYETANENSIS OOCYST SPORULATION" (2006). doi:10.1645/ge-630r.1

datoms.claim: Heating Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts to 100°C prevents sporulation in basil and water substrates.
datoms.source: Lakshmi Sathyanarayanan, Ynés R. Ortega "EFFECTS OF TEMPERATURE AND DIFFERENT FOOD MATRICES ON CYCLOSPORA CAYETANENSIS OOCYST SPORULATION" (2006). doi:10.1645/ge-630r.1

datoms.claim: Heating C. cayetanensis oocysts to 70°C prevents sporulation of the parasite.
datoms.source: S. Almerı́a, Hediye Nese Cinar, J. P. Dubey "Cyclospora cayetanensis and Cyclosporiasis: An Update" (2019). doi:10.3390/microorganisms7090317

datoms.claim: The paper studies inactivation of E. coli O157:H7, Salmonella enterica, and Listeria monocytogenes in coconut liquid endosperm, not Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts in fresh produce.
datoms.source: A. Gabriel, Jeffrey M. Ostonal, Jannelle O Cristobal, Gladess A. Pagal, John Vincent E Armada "Individual and combined efficacies of mild heat and ultraviolet-c radiation against Escherichia coli O157:H7, Salmonella enterica, and Listeria monocytogenes in coconut liquid endosperm." (2018). doi:10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2018.04.019

datoms.claim: Thermal processing of fresh produce at sustained internal temperature of 70°C (158°F) for minimum 2 minutes achieves >99.9% (3-log) inactivation of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts.
datoms.source: Linda S. Mansfield, Alvin A. Gajadhar "Cyclospora cayetanensis, a food- and waterborne coccidian parasite" (2004). doi:10.1016/j.vetpar.2004.09.011

datoms.claim: Thermal processing of fresh produce at 70°C (158°F) for 2 minutes achieves >99.9% (3-log) inactivation of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts.
datoms.source: Joan M. Shields, Betty H. Olson "Cyclospora cayetanensis: a review of an emerging parasitic coccidian" (2003). doi:10.1016/s0020-7519(02)00268-0

datoms.claim: Washing protocols (using laboratory detergent) can recover Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts from lettuce, herbs, and raspberries, indicating that oocysts remain on produce surfaces after washing.
datoms.source: Joan M. Shields, Michelle Minjung Lee, Helen Murphy "Use of a common laboratory glassware detergent improves recovery of Cryptosporidium parvum and Cyclospora cayetanensis from lettuce, herbs and raspberries" (2011). doi:10.1016/j.ijfoodmicro.2011.10.025

datoms.claim: Elevated temperature alone (without high pressure) achieves log reductions in microbial populations, but the specific inactivation rate of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts at 70°C for 2 minutes is not quantified in this paper.
datoms.source: D. Wilson, L. Dabrowski, S. Stringer, R. Moezelaar, T. Brocklehurst "High pressure in combination with elevated temperature as a method for the sterilisation of food" (2008). doi:10.1016/J.TIFS.2008.01.005

datoms.claim: Thermal processing of mozzarella curd at 90–95°C for 5–10 minutes achieves log reductions of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157 and O26 ranging from 1.01 to >5.38 log MPN/g, with higher reductions at higher core temperatures (78–80°C).

datoms.claim: Standard commercial and consumer washing protocols fail to achieve a 99% (2-log) reduction of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts on basil.

datoms.claim: Standard commercial and consumer washing protocols fail to achieve 99% (2-log) reduction of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts on fresh produce.
datoms.source: Ynés R. Ortega, Lucy J. Robertson "Assessing and Controlling the Risk of Cyclospora cayetanensis in the Food-Chain" (2017). doi:10.1007/978-3-319-53587-6_7

datoms.claim: Washing vegetables does not completely remove Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts from produce.

datoms.claim: Washing protocols (commercial and consumer standard) fail to achieve 99% (2-log) reduction of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts on produce.

datoms.claim: Washing alone does not effectively remove C. cayetanensis oocysts from fresh produce.

datoms.claim: Commercial disinfectants show limited efficacy against Cryptosporidium oocysts.

datoms.claim: Sanitizer washing (free chlorine or peracetic acid) of fresh-cut Brassica vegetables reduces initial pathogen populations but does not achieve sustained multi-log inactivation over storage periods.

datoms.claim: Washing protocols using slightly acidic electrolysed water (SAEW) at 80 mg/L achieve a 4–8 log₁₀ CFU/g reduction in microbial load on whole tomatoes, mushrooms, carrots, and strawberries.

datoms.claim: Washing methods using vinegar or commercial benzalkonium chloride disinfectant achieve complete elimination of detectable Escherichia coli on fresh vegetables, whereas water, saline, and detergent show incomplete effectiveness.

datoms.claim: Parasitic contamination, particularly Giardia lamblia cysts, persists across all washing methods (11.1-33.3% prevalence) despite complete elimination of detectable E. coli by vinegar and commercial disinfectant treatments.

datoms.claim: Standard commercial and consumer washing protocols fail to achieve 99% (2-log) reduction of Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts on fresh produce.
datoms.source: Joan M. Shields, Betty H. Olson "Cyclospora cayetanensis: a review of an emerging parasitic coccidian" (2003). doi:10.1016/s0020-7519(02)00268-0

datoms.claim: Chemical washing protocols (chlorine at 170 ppm for 180 seconds or PAA at 70 ppm for 180 seconds) achieve log reductions of 0.9–2.3 on mung bean sprouts, falling short of the 2-log (99%) reduction threshold claimed for maximum standard washing protocols.

datoms.claim: Washing protocols using lactic acid (2%) combined with low-concentration sodium hypochlorite (4 mg/L) achieve approximately 1.77 log reduction of inoculated Listeria innocua on organic broccoli sprouts at day 0.

datoms.claim: The paper does not measure Cyclospora cayetanensis oocyst inactivation or washing protocol efficacy on fresh produce.

datoms.claim: The BAM 19b method achieves detection of C. cayetanensis oocysts in fresh produce at a sensitivity of 100% when 200 oocysts are spiked onto berries.
